Malcolm X. The Muslim minister and human rights activist who challenged the integrationist strategy of the Civil Rights Movement, advocating instead for Black nationalism, self-determination, and armed self-defense. His fiery rhetoric and uncompromising stance on racial dignity made him an iconic figure and a controversial counterpoint to Martin Luther King Jr. He joined the Nation of Islam while imprisoned and became one of its most charismatic ministers, serving as the organization's spokesman by the late nineteen-fifties. He called for Black separatism and the creation of an independent Black nation within America, rejecting integration as a goal. He advocated by any means necessary, a phrase that signaled willingness to use force in self-defense, contrasting sharply with King's philosophy of nonviolence. In 1964 he briefly met with King, but their ideological differences remained unbridged. That same year he left the Nation of Islam and founded the Organization of Afro-American Unity, which took a broader pan-African and internationalist stance. He traveled to Mecca and Africa in 1964, experiences that moderated his earlier strict separatism and expanded his vision of Black liberation. On February 21, 1965 he was assassinated in New York by Nation of Islam members, though questions about the full circumstances persist. His rivalry with King defined the era's debate over tactics and goals, and like Booker T. Washington before him, he advocated Black self-reliance, though grounded in very different ideology. His posthumously published autobiography remains foundational to understanding Black radical thought.
